text: 75TH ANNIVERSARY INTRODUCTION Most of us first encountered George Orwell’s work as adolescents when we were assigned his 1945 novel Animal Farm in school. I distinctly remember being as enchanted by the talking animals as I was inspired by the power of metaphor and allegory. Could literature actually do that? Could it weave something magically spellbinding while critiquing society at the same time? My own teenager unequivocally declared Animal Farm, was her favorite novel in middle school. Though many years have passed since those early days of falling in love with books, I still seek that thrill of discovery, that leap of the heart that happens when I’m captivated by a story. It’s even better when a wide audience of readers shares the experience with me. To those of us elated by Animal Farm, my dedicated teacher in the Memphis public schools said 1984 was the next novel by Orwell that we should read, though it was far less often assigned. I didn’t read it until graduate school, and I remember thinking about how it resembled and differed from Animal Farm. In both novels Orwell’s satiric voice veers between cautionary and caustic, but in 1984 his dystopian vision had deepened, his perspective broadened. If Animal Farm was a specific critique of the events leading up to the Russian Revolution, 1984 expanded into a more wide-ranging criticism of what might happen if a totalitarian government took complete control. That layered complexity has given Orwell’s last published novel “legs,” as some might put it. Since its publication seventy-five years ago, it has inspired innumerable essays analyzing everything from the three slogans of the Party—War is Peace, Freedom is Slavery, Ignorance is Strength—to its predictions about the death of language and ideas. It is most certainly a testament to Orwell’s accomplishment that the novel has fruitfully inspired nearly a century of close readings. Recently, however, I read 1984 alone, without the benefits of a classroom setting. I wanted to imagine myself as a new reader. How might I feel about this book if I didn’t know it as a classic text? What if I wandered into the bookstore and picked it up because I thought the premise was intriguing? I know, I know. This feels like an impossible hypothetical. Everyone knows 1984 is canonical. Yet when I asked around recently, most of my friends admitted that they’d either never read the novel or hadn’t read it in many years. So perhaps this idea isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds. Let’s try it. Let’s enter the Orwellian universe as if for the first time. I pick up the book and begin to read the first pages. When the novel opens, Winston Smith has been summoned to help a neighbor unclog her sink in their decaying apartment building ironically named Victory Mansions. Though he is only thirty-nine years old, we learn that he has a varicose ulcer on his leg. He lives alone and works for the government. The details feel banal, quotidian. But then this ordinariness is immediately shot through with weirdness: there are two-way telescreens everywhere, and Winston must meticulously guard his thoughts and movements or he could be apprehended by the Thought Police. The Thought Police? There is something wildly imaginative about these opening pages, and I am both intrigued and horrified. In an era of nearly ubiquitous cameras and facial recognition technology and social media. I am no stranger to the loss of privacy. But Orwell’s portrayal of thought surveillance boggles the mind. He writes that “even a back can be revealing.” To add to this terror, Winston is guilty of more than just a thoughtcrime\ he has written down his heresy. I must keep reading to find out more. But, first, I do something I often do when I’m a chapter or two into a book. I flip to the back cover and read the details again. The book was published in 1949, but the novel is set in 1984. thirty-five years later. I glance at the author’s biographical details and learn that Orwell was dead by 1950. Remember. I am imagining myself encountering the book for the first time. I am just realizing that Orwell died at forty-six years old. Had he lived to a not-unreasonable eighty-one, he would have been able to witness firsthand which path the world would take by 1984. I understand in those opening pages that I am reading a dystopian novel, an imagined future in which government surveillance constricts and defines people’s lives. It’s a strange orientation because I am reading it at a time beyond 1984 and can therefore measure what Orwell guessed correctly about the future while also noting his contemporaneous perspective. Orwell presciently addresses his conundrum in the first chapter. “How could you communicate with the future? It was of its nature impossible. Either the future would resemble the present in which case it would not listen to him. or it would be different from it, and his predicament would be meaningless.” Yet I would argue that it is precisely because of the novel’s longevity that he manages to speak to the future. And its longevity is partially due to his prescience. I write historical novels, which means I spend a lot of time in library archives. Examining old letters or maps or diaries transports me. Once you’ve experienced this, you know that history is not really past. We can relive historical moments, a feeling that is nothing short of mystical. I think the same is true of the future. In dystopian fiction, writers journey into their imagined worlds. Orwell speaks to us because his imagination allowed him to move through time. Writers (and readers!) are true time travelers with access to the portal. Now that Orwell has established this ordinary but weird world, one not entirely dissimilar to my own, I begin to connect to the humans who populate it.
